text.p: Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said a steeper cut in interest rates would have been "irresponsible" in light of the fact that inflation is expected to surpass the government's 1996 target.

"I believe a more significant reduction in interest rates would have been irresponsible. It would have fueled inflation and would not contribute to the profitability of the business sector," Frenkel told Reuters.

Earlier on Tuesday the central bank announced it would lower its key lending rate for October by 0.3 percentage points to an an annualised 15.5 percent. The Bank of Israel attributed its decision to the low consumer price indices in the past two months and a rate of expansion in money supply in line with expected growth.
On the other hand, the capital market's inflationary expectations for the coming 12 months and forecasts for inflation in 1996 are above the government's target of 8-10 percent for this year.
"It looks now that during 1996 inflation will exceed the level set by the government," Frenkel said.
While the inflation rate in the second half of the year is expected to be significantly lower than in the first half of the year, Frenkel said it would be "imprudent to declare victory prematurely".
Nevertheless, the business sector said on Tuesday a bigger rate cut was needed.

"In assessing monetary policy I believe we should not look at a single step like today's step but rather cumulative steps that have taken place recently. Interest rates have declined 1.5 percentage points since August. That's a very significant decline," Frenkel said.

"The choice for Israel today should not be stated simply as between low and high interest rates but rather as between lower or higher inflation. In this choice the Bank of Israel opted for a lower inflation."
The biggest problem facing Israel's economy is the widening current account deficit in the balance of payments, he said.

"This deficit reflects the basic fact that Israel's total expenditures in the private and public sector exceed total income and the only effective way to deal with this gap is by cutting government expenditures," Frenkel said.
The government has already approved a 4.9 billion shekel cut in the 1997 budget, which the Knesset (parliament) must approve.
"It is now imperative that this decision is adopted as soon as possible by our Knesset and implemented also as soon as possible," Frenkel said.

"Furthermore, in view of the growing discrepancy of the budget deficit from the planned trajectory it would also be highly desirable if the government found additional ways to cut spending beyond those that have already been decided upon."
